data.title: Classic budgeting rules don't work anymore - -2-
data.description:
The 5% of income left over would need to cover a lot, including student loan and other debt payments and nonessentials like subscriptions, clothing and gifts. It would also have to cover things like paying for vacations, replenishing an emergency fund if it's been tapped, and setting aside money in a health savings or college account.

With $417 a month to spend, a family would likely not be able to afford all these things. Paying off high-interest debt would be the priority.

This simple budget illustrates how difficult it can be for families with young children to save 15% for the future while managing their spending today.

To cover their basic expenses, Emerson said, many of her clients have to temporarily reduce their 401(k) contributions for a few years before their children start school. "While not ideal - and generally I try to encourage clients to reduce discretionary expenses first - sometimes it's the only option," she said.

If parents must lower their retirement contributions during those lean years, financial experts recommend they at least put in enough to get their company's full match, if one is offered, because that match is part of their compensation.

Look at housing and transportation to make big changes

On average, housing and transportation alone account for about half of household spending. Decisions about these two budget items can have huge effects on how much is left for a family to spend on everything else.

"If you're spending more in those categories, it's going to come around on the back side to impact you, potentially in a negative way," Watts said.

Making the choice to live in a smaller home or in a different neighborhood, or to drive an older car or only have one vehicle for the household, can save hundreds of dollars that can then be spent on other things the family needs or wants.

There may not be many other areas where a family making $100,000 can cut back, financial planners told MarketWatch. Gaining financial flexibility then requires increasing income, for example through a side hustle, a raise or a new job.

Lock in expenses, even as income rises

Over time, bonuses and raises add up, and the trick is to avoid lifestyle creep as your disposable income increases, Grant said. Lock in whatever expenses you can. "Some things are going to rise with inflation, but not everything," he said. "So try to control what you can control."

Married couples with children had a median income of about $130,000 in 2024, giving them more leeway than the family in the budget outlined above. One-parent families, however, earned significantly less.

Based on a gross income of $130,000, contributing 15% toward retirement would add up to $19,500 per year for a couple.

Locking in the modest spending levels (in dollars) from the budget above would mean spending 17% of gross income on housing, 5% on transportation, 5% on food, 5% on healthcare and 10% on childcare. In order to save money and have enough for discretionary items, it may be more helpful to maintain these spending levels than to use the well-known rules of thumb.

Accounting for taxes on the $130,000, the family would have about $1,700 per month, or roughly 15% of gross income, for things like debt payments; spending on subscriptions, shopping, gifts, dining out and vacations; replenishing emergency funds; and setting money aside in health savings or college accounts.

This is more in line with popular budgeting assumptions for "wants" and can only be achieved if the family can find ways to spend far less on their basic needs than common spending guidelines allow for.

"What we're doing by setting these rules of thumb is establishing what our standard of living can be," Watts said. Even families with typical incomes cannot afford their ideal standard of living in all categories, he noted, so they need to focus on "spending on what matters most to them."

You can write to us at readerstories@marketwatch.com. A reporter may be in touch to learn more. MarketWatch will not attribute your answers to you by name without your permission.

-Venessa Wong

data.title: ARIDGE and UAE Authorities to Jointly Establish the World's First Personal Flying Car Regulatory Sandbox
data.description:
ARIDGE and UAE Authorities to Jointly Establish the World's First Personal Flying Car Regulatory Sandbox

ARIDGE and UAE Authorities to Jointly Establish the World's First Personal Flying Car Regulatory Sandbox

PR Newswire

RAS AL KHAIMAH, UAE, Sept. 19, 2026

Company deepens its UAE presence through flight validation, airworthiness activities and preparations for future inter-emirate advanced air mobility services.

RAS AL KHAIMAH, UAE, Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ARIDGE (Formerly XPENG AEROHT), Asia's largest flying car company, officially signed a strategic cooperation agreement with the Emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, United Arab Emirates. In the presence of His Highness Sheikh Saud bin Saqr Al Qasimi, UAE Supreme Council Member and Ruler of Ras Al Khaimah, and under the full oversight of the UAE General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), the two parties will jointly establish an Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) regulatory sandbox in the UAE, while simultaneously advancing the planning and implementation of an inter-emirate demonstration route connecting Abu Dhabi and Ras Al Khaimah.

The cooperation marks a major industry breakthrough, making ARIDGE the first Chinese flying car company to enter a national-level regulatory sandbox in the Middle East, while also establishing the world's first flying car testing sandbox dedicated to personal low-altitude flight.

Through the regulatory sandbox led by RAKTA (Ras Al Khaimah Transport Authority), ARIDGE will conduct flight validation under desert conditions, evaluate aircraft performance across representative operational scenarios and refine procedures within controlled airspace. The program will provide a structured environment for the company to validate its technology and operating model while working closely with relevant authorities and industry partners.

The planned Abu Dhabi–Ras Al Khaimah demonstration route will serve as a real-world platform for assessing the requirements of future inter-emirate advanced air mobility services. The program is expected to cover key operational areas, including flight planning, airspace coordination, ground support, passenger handling, aircraft turnaround and safety management.

By combining aircraft validation, regulatory engagement and route-based operational testing, ARIDGE aims to build a comprehensive foundation for the safe and compliant introduction of commercial air-mobility services in the UAE. His Highness Sheikh Saud said: "The true value of technology lies in the difference it makes to people's lives and in its ability to support development and improve services." He noted that "Ras Al Khaimah is harnessing innovation and new technologies to support the growth of its economy, enhance quality of life, strengthen the Emirate's competitiveness and reinforce its position as a preferred destination to live, work, invest and visit."

As part of its recent activities in the UAE, ARIDGE also conducted a live formation flight demonstration of its modular flying car, the Land Aircraft Carrier, at a reception hosted by the Chinese Embassy celebrating the 77th Anniversary of the Founding of the People's Republic of China and the 42nd Anniversary of the Establishment of Diplomatic Relations between China and the UAE at the Emirates Palace, Abu Dhabi. Attended by the Chinese Ambassador Zeng Jixin, and representatives of the UAE government and business community, as well as international guests, the demonstration offered partners a firsthand view of ARIDGE's technology.

The Land Aircraft Carrier embodies ARIDGE's vision of integrating ground and air tourism into a flexible solution. Its modular configuration is designed to expand the practical applications of ground and air vehicles while creating new possibilities for how people experience the sky. With safety at its core, ARIDGE's advanced flight control system allows pilots to override autonomous functions while maintaining stable flight within safe parameters. The air module includes fully redundant systems for propulsion, power, communications, and flight control, with automatic rotor failure response in milliseconds.

ARIDGE's entry into the regulatory sandbox and advancement of the demonstration route mark an important step in its global expansion. The UAE program will generate valuable operational experience and support ARIDGE in developing localized, scalable advanced air mobility services, while accelerating the company's broader global expansion across key international markets, including Europe and Southeast Asia.

data.title: Traditional bond investors have lost money for years. These five-star portfolio managers show a better way.
data.description:
By Philip van Doorn

A narrow focus on investment-grade bonds can lead to dismal returns, says Morgan Stanley's fixed-income team

For better long-term returns in the bond market, investors need variety, according to portfolio managers at Morgan Stanley.

With 10-year U.S. Treasury yields now above 5%, investors are looking at new opportunities for attractive income streams away from the stock market.

However, predicting interest rates and bond prices is a challenge, while sticking with U.S. Treasury paper or investment-grade bonds could mean missing out on opportunities for much better long-term returns, according to portfolio managers at Morgan Stanley.

"Traditional core aggregate bond investors have been losing money cumulatively for five years, and there is a better way to bond invest," Andrew Szczurowski, the co-head of the mortgage and securitized-investment team at Morgan Stanley, said during an interview with MarketWatch, which included his colleagues Brian Shaw, Justin Bourgette and Chip Driscoll, all of whom work on the team managing the $20 billion Eaton Vance Strategic Income Fund ESIIX.

The fund is rated five stars (the highest rating) within Morningstar's multisector-bond category. Morgan Stanley acquired Eaton Vance in 2021.

This chart illustrates Szczurowski's point:

For five years through Sept. 14, total returns were negative for indexes of 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds and investment-grade corporate bonds.

The Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index of investment-grade corporate bonds has declined nearly 3% with interest reinvested over the past five years, while the S&P U.S. Treasury Bond 10-year Index has declined 12.4%. Meanwhile, the Bloomberg U.S. Corporate High Yield Index of bonds rated below investment grade has returned 20.8%, and the VanEck J.P. Morgan EM Local Currency Bond ETF EMLC, which tracks the J.P. Morgan GBI-EM Global Core Index of bonds in emerging markets, has returned 10%.

Rising interest rates have taken their toll on the higher-quality bond indexes. The riskier bond pools have been much better performers despite facing a higher risk of default and potentially greater price sensitivity as market conditions evolve.

The Eaton Vance Strategic Income Fund has outperformed them all, with a five-year return of 29.7%, after fund expenses (which total 0.74% of assets annually with a temporary partial waiver of 0.50%) and any credit losses.

In addition to high-yield corporates, Shaw cited three themes that have helped the Morgan Stanley team achieve strong long-term performance for the fund:

-- Investing in debt of distressed companies or governments. Fire-sale prices mean much higher yields with the hope that prices will recover as the issuers' fortunes improve.

-- Frontier local-market investing. These are markets that aren't yet included in emerging-markets indexes. While he couldn't name current investments, Shaw mentioned Serbia as an example of a country that had been considered to be a frontier market before political reforms caused its government bonds to be added to the GBI-EM index in June 2021.

-- "Market-friendly political shifts," including recent election results in Hungary and Colombia. "We took positions with the expectation that the market-friendly candidate would win in both countries," Shaw said. "Those have been accretive to the portfolio this year."

data.title: Most workers would take a pay cut for job security right now: 'I can't deal with this stress anymore'
data.description:
By Weston Blasi

Workers used to want higher salaries and flexibility, but now they're chasing a sense of safety

Workers used to chase higher pay and flexibility. Now they're chasing something else.

For decades, the standard career advice was to follow the money. Now, it's about finding job security.

Monster's recent "2026 Job Security Report" found that more than half of U.S. workers would accept a pay cut for a greater sense of job security, and 61% said they'd give up at least one aspect of their compensation or their workplace experience - like bonuses, perks and other incentives - if it made them feel more secure in their role.

What's more, the survey found workers would take pretty sizable pay cuts to keep working: 26% would take a pay cut of up to 5%, and another 28% would be willing to be paid 5% less or more - including 11% who would accept a pay cut greater than 10%.

"Job security seems to be a top priority for workers," Monster career expert Vicki Salemi told MarketWatch. "That doesn't mean that flexibility and work-life balance are no longer important, but things have shifted."

What exactly have they shifted from? Compensation was always a major priority for workers, and still is. But in the years following the COVID pandemic work-from-home boom, flexibility became an increasingly important part of the bargain. This even led to viral discussions about whether a $240,000 salaried job in-person, or a $120,000 salaried job fully remote was better.

Things have changed. "In the years before, the deal was quite simple: If you don't like your job, you can leave and land somewhere better in 5-6 weeks," Jan Hendrik von Ahlen, a managing director and employment expert at JobLeads, told MarketWatch. "Job security was all about your skills and experience that would land you a new opportunity, not about your employer. In 2026, it's pretty much gone."

Unemployment was just above 3% during parts of 2022, for example, during one of the hottest labor markets in decades. The latest unemployment reading from August was 4.1% - which is still a relatively low figure from a historical perspective, but it's a cooler job market than previous years, particularly for recent college graduates. The labor market may also be impacted going forward by possible Federal Reserve rate hikes, which are widely expected.

"A job search now takes three to six months, and it's normal to send more than 100 applications to barely hear anything back," von Ahlen added.

One of those workers who thinks job security is paramount is Arkadiusz Bolanowski, 32, a Colorado man who works in solar development and an independent power producer.

He moved over from working in commercial finance three years ago, because he believed the solar industry's rapid growth would keep him safe from layoffs.

"I think safety is more industry-specific than company-specific. If I get fired, downsized, restructured, I feel like I have the ability to find another job within the industry," Bolanowski said. "Working in energy right now feels secure with the growing demand due to load growth from data centers."

'Once you've lived through losing a job ... a bigger paycheck stops being the deciding factor.' Chelsea Jay, a recruiter and professional career coach at ResumeCoach

And job recruiters told MarketWatch that they are seeing plenty of evidence that job hunters are seeking security.

"I've worked with clients this year who chose a lower salary because the role felt more stable," Chelsea Jay, a recruiter and professional career coach at ResumeCoach, told MarketWatch. She said most of these clients had been laid off within the past couple of years, which changed their perspective. "Once you've lived through losing a job ... a bigger paycheck stops being the deciding factor," she said.

And when her clients are weighing an offer that pays more against an offer that pays less but comes from a company with a steadier track record, fewer rounds of cuts and more consistent hiring, then "more often than not, they're choosing the steadier one," she added.

Related: Want to land more job interviews? Stop letting AI write your résumé.

Measuring how safe or secure a job is is not exactly a science, but there are a few things you can seek out.

"There's no perfect way to measure it, but there are real signs, and most people ignore them until it's too late," Jay said.

In addition to looking for growth industries, like Bolanowski did, Jay advises workers to watch how the company talks, not just what it says. "If leadership gets vague the moment someone asks about headcount or budget, pay attention to that," she said

Some other signs that you may lack job security in your industry or company include a role sitting empty for months after somebody quits, or a large portion of your workload being susceptible to AI advancements, Jay said.

"Look at how much of your day-to-day could be handled by a tool or an automated process," Jay said. "That's not a reason to panic. It's a reason to start building the parts of your job that require judgment, relationships, and taste - the things AI still can't do."

'I can't deal with this stress anymore. I'd rather take a massive pay cut.'A tech worker who asked to remain anonymous

One tech worker, who spoke with MarketWatch anonymously over fears that he may be part of some upcoming layoffs at his company, said he is questioning his own job security in this way.

"We've seen an unprecedented number of layoffs in the technology sector as economic factors combined with 'AI hype' have led to significant downsizing. Many of those who were laid off left tech entirely to pursue careers viewed as safer," said the worker, a male in his 30s.

So he's got one foot out the door, too. "No one in this industry feels safe, even in organizations more resilient to these layoffs," he said. "If I lose this job, absolutely, this is my last go in this industry."

He's been so rocked by recent tech layoffs over the past few years that he began taking part-time nursing classes at a local community college. It's the safest career path he could think of considering the strong demand for workers in the healthcare industry in recent years.

And AI fears over job security are not just theoretical. Many companies have publicly said that some of their recent layoffs were at least somewhat related to AI, including Oracle( ORCL), Amazon( AMZN), Cloudflare(NET), and Block (XYZ).

Hence why that tech worker said he is completely done with the industry, and would welcome taking less money by becoming a nurse.

"I can't deal with this stress anymore. I'd rather take a massive pay cut, and have to deal with all manner of abuse and bodily fluid. Genuinely," he said. "It's better than knowing your entire life can fall apart overnight at the whim of some person purchasing their third mansion."

-Weston Blasi

data.title: Want Your Own Barrel of Bourbon? BarrelPick.com Launches at Kentucky Bourbon Festival
data.description:
Want Your Own Barrel of Bourbon? BarrelPick.com Launches at Kentucky Bourbon Festival

Want Your Own Barrel of Bourbon? BarrelPick.com Launches at Kentucky Bourbon Festival

PR Newswire

BARDSTOWN, Ky., Sept. 19, 2026

New platform gives bourbon enthusiasts the ability to buy a full barrel of bourbon, continue aging it and ultimately create their own private single-barrel release.

BARDSTOWN, Ky., Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- BarrelPick.com, a new platform designed to make full-barrel bourbon ownership accessible to individual consumers, officially launched this month during the Kentucky Bourbon Festival in Bardstown, Kentucky.

The platform allows individuals to purchase an entire barrel of bourbon, keep it aging in Kentucky, follow its development over time and ultimately determine when and how it will be bottled.

Rather than selecting a finished bourbon from a retail shelf, BarrelPick.com gives consumers the opportunity to enter the process years earlier and make decisions traditionally handled by whiskey producers and private barrel programs.

"Most people experience bourbon only after every important decision has already been made," said Steve Scheidecker, founder of BarrelPick.com. "We wanted to give people the opportunity to experience bourbon from the other side of the barrel. You can choose the whiskey, follow it as it ages and ultimately decide what that barrel becomes."

Bringing Barrel Ownership Directly to Consumers

BarrelPick.com was created as a dedicated marketplace and management platform for individual barrel ownership.

The company provides access to aged and newly filled barrels from whiskey producers across the United States, with inventory ranging from recently filled bourbon to barrels that have spent more than a decade aging in oak.

After purchasing a barrel, owners can choose to continue aging it or begin the bottling process. Owners can select the proof of the finished whiskey, develop their bottle and label design, and create a private single-barrel release from their bourbon.

Owners also have the option to bottle only a portion of a barrel, beginning with as few as 48 bottles, while allowing the remaining whiskey to continue aging.

BarrelPick.com currently lists more than 1,000 barrels from more than 20 distilleries and producers.

The concept is intended for bourbon enthusiasts as well as families, companies, clubs and organizations looking to create a whiskey tied to a particular person, place or milestone.

"A barrel can spend years developing before it ever reaches a bottle," Scheidecker said. "Owning one gives you something a bottle never can: time. You get to decide whether to bottle it now, give it another year or continue following it as it changes."

A Kentucky Home for Every Barrel

A key component of the BarrelPick.com platform is its Kentucky-based storage and bottling infrastructure.

BarrelPick.com has partnered with Kentucky Artisan Distillery in Crestwood, Kentucky, just outside Louisville, to provide storage and bottling services for participating barrels.

Through the platform, owners can track their barrel, view specifications and status, request samples and begin the bottling process when they are ready.

The company also coordinates the compliance and logistics required to move a barrel from acquisition through eventual bottling.

Launching During Bourbon's Biggest Week

BarrelPick.com made its public debut in conjunction with the 2026 Kentucky Bourbon Festival in Bardstown.

The annual festival, held in the Bourbon Capital of the World, brings together bourbon producers, industry leaders and enthusiasts from around the world. Tickets to the 2026 festival sold out for the fifth consecutive year.

BarrelPick.com introduced the platform to festival attendees through its presence on the festival grounds, where guests could taste single-barrel bourbon from the company's inventory, view examples of customized bottle designs and learn how full-barrel ownership works.

The company also offered limited BarrelPick.com Sample Sets featuring five barrel-strength single-barrel samples pulled directly from inventory.

Ahead of the festival, BarrelPick.com hosted its inaugural Single Barrel Showcase at Kentucky Artisan Distillery in Crestwood. Guests toured the bottling operation, tasted bourbon directly from barrels in the warehouse and received a behind-the-scenes look at the process of taking a single barrel from the rickhouse to a finished private release.

The launch comes as bourbon tourism continues to attract millions of visitors to Kentucky. The Kentucky Distillers' Association reported that Kentucky Bourbon Trail experiences welcomed approximately 2.7 million visitors in 2025.

From Barrel to Bottle

BarrelPick.com is designed to manage the process from the initial barrel selection through bottling.

Owners can browse available barrels, select a specific barrel, allow it to continue aging, request samples and eventually choose how their bourbon will be bottled.

When the owner decides the barrel is ready, options include barrel-strength bottling or proofing the whiskey to a selected strength. Owners can then create a bottle and label design for their private release.

Unlike an investment offering, BarrelPick.com is designed around ownership and consumption of the physical product. Customers purchase a specific barrel of bourbon with the intention of ultimately having the whiskey bottled for personal use.

"Bourbon has always been about patience, place and the people behind it," Scheidecker said. "BarrelPick.com gives more people the opportunity to become part of that process instead of simply seeing the finished product."

About BarrelPick.com

BarrelPick.com is a dedicated platform for bourbon and whiskey barrel ownership, providing individuals, families, businesses and organizations access to full barrels from producers across the United States. The platform brings barrel selection, secure storage, sampling, aging, bottle design, bottling and compliance into a single experience.

BarrelPick.com currently provides access to more than 1,000 aged and new-fill barrels from more than 20 distilleries and producers, with Kentucky-based storage and bottling available through its partnership with Kentucky Artisan Distillery.

For more information, visit BarrelPick.com.

data.title: Qatar Foundation - Wilton Park Dialogue Calls for Global Action to Drive Social Development Through Sport
data.description:
Qatar Foundation - Wilton Park Dialogue Calls for Global Action to Drive Social Development Through Sport

Qatar Foundation - Wilton Park Dialogue Calls for Global Action to Drive Social Development Through Sport

PR Newswire

WEST SUSSEX, England, Sept. 19, 2026

Three-day UK dialogue emphasizes female empowerment, inclusion, and systemic reform across the Global South.

WEST SUSSEX, England, Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- International leaders spanning government, policy, development, and sport convened at Wilton Park for a three-day dialogue hosted with Qatar Foundation (QF), calling for a global coalition to turn sport's potential to support social development into practical action.

Held under the theme 'Sport for Development in the Global South: Advancing Female Empowerment, Inclusion, and Accessibility', the event focused on removing structural barriers to sporting opportunity for women and girls, building on UN Resolution 59/17, initiated by Qatar with Indonesia and Morocco and co-sponsored by 71 nations. Wilton Park and QF will now jointly develop an actionable roadmap for action in policy, coaching, and infrastructure.

Speaking at the dialogue, Her Excellency Sheikha Hind bint Hamad Al Thani, Vice Chairperson of Qatar Foundation, urged action that goes beyond basic parity, saying: "The barriers girls face are fundamentally different. "Our approach is to close that gap in practice, not just in principle: involving women in the design of facilities, providing coaching tailored to women's needs, and building the scientific research base that, too often, doesn't exist for women's and girls' sport."

His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, President-Elect of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly, told the dialogue that sport "changes how a girl is seen by her family and community, and how she sees herself", saying: "A girl who plays on a team learns to lead, to fail and try again in public — and that confidence follows her into the classroom, workplace, and civic life."

Participants in the dialogue included Olympism365, Special Olympics, Laureus Sport for Good, NBA Africa, FIVB, and Olympic athletes Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce and Ibtihaj Muhammad.

QF continues to advance inclusive sport, with over 70,000 female participants participating in tailored sporting activities at the Education City Stadium in the past two years, and its Circle In initiative supporting sport-for-development projects in 10 countries.

About Qatar Foundation

Qatar Foundation for Education, Science and Community Development (QF) is a non-profit organization driving education, research, and community development. Founded in 1995, QF operates an interconnected ecosystem at Education City in Doha, Qatar, empowering individuals and driving positive social change. Visit www.qf.org.qa.

Med Spa Expert Lindsey Smith Explains What to Expect From a First Med Spa Visit in HelloNation

Med Spa Expert Lindsey Smith Explains What to Expect From a First Med Spa Visit in HelloNation

PR Newswire

BRYANT, Ark., Sept. 19, 2026

The article explains how consultations, medical history reviews, treatment planning, and clear communication help patients prepare for their first med spa visit.

BRYANT, Ark., Sept. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should patients expect during their first med spa visit in Bryant, Arkansas? According to a HelloNation article, Lindsey Smith of Flawless Med Spa in Bryant, Arkansas, provides practical guidance on how a first visit consultation helps set the foundation for safe, personalized care. The article explains that understanding what happens during the initial appointment allows patients to feel informed and confident before starting any treatment.

The HelloNation feature describes a med spa as a blend of medical expertise and spa comfort. Lindsey Smith explains that a professional med spa offers clinical-grade services such as injectables, laser treatments, and body contouring in a welcoming, nonintimidating environment. The goal is to provide visible improvement while ensuring patients understand each step of their care. The first visit is designed to build trust and clarity, helping patients feel comfortable asking questions about their treatment plan and expected results.

A first visit usually begins with a conversation about patient goals. The HelloNation article notes that providers take time to learn what changes matter most, such as improving skin texture, addressing fine lines, or targeting stubborn areas through body contouring. Lindsey Smith emphasizes that no two patients share the same priorities, which is why a customized plan is essential. Understanding these goals helps providers select noninvasive procedures that align with both expectations and lifestyle.

Medical history also plays a critical role. Even when treatments are noninvasive, providers must review allergies, medications, and prior procedures to prevent unwanted reactions. Lindsey Smith explains that detailed medical information allows the provider to recommend treatments safely and effectively. Patients are often surprised by how thorough these questions can be, but careful screening helps create the right balance between safety and results.

During the consultation, many med spas in Bryant, Arkansas, also take baseline photos. As the HelloNation article explains, these images are used solely to track progress and maintain accuracy over time. Lindsey Smith notes that photos help patients see subtle improvements that may not be obvious from memory alone. They also allow providers to adjust the treatment plan if results develop differently than expected. This documentation process reinforces that care is personalized and professionally monitored.

Clear communication is one of the most valuable parts of the first visit. Lindsey Smith highlights that providers should explain each treatment option in straightforward terms, covering what it does, how it feels, and what kind of outcome to expect. The HelloNation feature points out that this approach helps patients make decisions based on understanding rather than impulse. When patients know the difference between short-term and long-term results, they can plan accordingly and feel more confident about their investment in wellness.

Downtime is another key topic during the first med spa visit. Lindsey Smith advises that even noninvasive procedures can cause brief redness, mild swelling, or temporary sensitivity. Providers explain how long recovery may take and what aftercare instructions to follow. According to the HelloNation article, receiving written or digital aftercare instructions helps patients maintain results and avoid unnecessary discomfort. Proper care after treatment reinforces safety and improves overall satisfaction.

Budget and timing are also discussed during the first appointment. Some treatments require multiple sessions spaced over several weeks to achieve optimal results. Lindsey Smith explains that by outlining the expected number of visits and the spacing between them, providers help patients plan both financially and logistically. The HelloNation feature clarifies that this conversation is not about sales pressure but about transparency, so patients fully understand how long their treatment plan may take.

Many first-time visitors to a med spa feel nervous about discomfort or pain. Lindsey Smith acknowledges this and assures patients that providers take time to explain what sensations to expect and what comfort options are available. Modern technology in med spas is designed to minimize discomfort without compromising results. The HelloNation article adds that when patients know how long a session will last and what it will feel like, the experience feels far less intimidating.

Trust forms the foundation of every successful med spa experience. Lindsey Smith points out that open communication allows patients to feel heard and respected. Providers who listen carefully and answer questions honestly build long-term relationships with their patients. The HelloNation article highlights that this trust transforms the first visit into a collaborative process where both patient and provider work toward shared goals.

By the end of the appointment, patients should have a clear understanding of their options, the timeline for results, and how to care for their skin or body after treatment. Lindsey Smith explains that a first med spa visit should feel like the start of a guided partnership rather than a one-time procedure. In Bryant, more med spas are adopting this educational and transparent approach, ensuring that every new patient feels prepared and supported from the very beginning.

What to Expect From Your First Med Spa Visit in Bryant, AR features insights from Lindsey Smith, Med Spa Expert of Bryant, AR, in HelloNation.

data.title: Warsh's Fed shows it's serious about taming inflation. Why Wall Street now believes it.
data.description:
By Jeffry Bartash

The Federal Reserve hasn't met its 2% inflation goal in five years

Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh is trying to drag U.S. inflation back down to prepandemic levels. How long will it take?

After more than five years of failing to do so, Federal Reserve leaders think they can shrink the rate of inflation to 2% by 2029 with just slightly higher U.S. interest rates. Are they serious?

They are. And most economists and financial professionals are now inclined to believe them.

"We can definitely get to 2% inflation in two years' time," said chief economist Gregory Daco of EY Parthenon.

The initial step was the first increase in interest rates in three years, and it came under a new chairman picked by President Donald Trump, who has demanded the Fed slash borrowing costs instead. Kevin Warsh, who took the helm at the central bank in May, regained badly needed credibility with the hike after a shaky start to his tenure.

Warsh and the Fed still need a lot of help, however.

The effects of the Trump administration's 2025 tariffs have mostly faded, but flareups in trade disputes like the one with Canada could create additional roadblocks on the path to 2% inflation.

The protracted war with Iran also has to end to allow oil and gas prices to return to relatively low preconflict levels. Surging energy prices pushed the rate of inflation above 4% again in the spring and are probably the biggest obstacle for the Fed.

Quickly getting back to 2% might sound improbable, but many economists point out that the yearly rate of inflation, using the Fed's preferred price gauge, had slowed to 2.3% in April 2025, just as Trump's tariffs upended a decades-old global trading system.

"The Fed was on track to get to 2% before the tariffs," said Stephen Douglas, chief economist at NISA Investment Advisors. "We think inflation is going to return to the low 2% range over the next few years largely on its own."

Warsh rights the ship

Just a month ago, Wall Street had plenty of doubts.

In his first few months on the job, Warsh insisted the central bank would return the U.S. to an era of low inflation like the one that persisted before the pandemic. Yet he also seemed reluctant to take the necessary steps.

All of that began to change a few weeks ago. First Warsh gave a big speech at the end of August signaling he was unhappy about stubbornly high inflation. Investors took that as a cue he really would raise interest rates.

Then on Wednesday, the Warsh-led Fed pulled the trigger, raising a key short-term interest rate for the first time since mid-2023 and signaling at least one additional rate hike - and possibly more - to come.

Higher interest rates are a time-tested tool to tame inflation. By raising borrowing costs, they slow the economy and ease demand for goods, services and labor.

One rate hike alone, or even two, probably won't be enough to slay the inflation beast, given the tail effects of the tariffs and high oil prices. What mattered most on Wednesday was that Warsh gave Wall Street a reason to believe he was serious.

"Whether the Fed or investors think 2% [inflation] is attainable is secondary to his message," said Will Compernolle, macroeconomic strategist at FHN Financial. "He was able to convince markets he was going to do what it takes to bring inflation down."

Supply and demand

Whatever Warsh's intentions, higher interest rates can only do so much.

The most recent bout of high inflation, like runaway prices in the pandemic era, is the result of what economists call "supply shocks." And supply shocks are almost impossible for the Fed to control, as Warsh admitted.

"We cannot affect any individual price, whether it be oil prices, whether it be foodstuffs at the grocery store," he said Wednesday after the Fed rate hike was announced.

The tariffs, for instance, made it more costly for businesses to obtain supplies. And the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz reduced the supply of oil around the world.

"Interest rates can cool demand. They cannot lower a tariff, reopen a shipping lane, or bring down the price of a barrel of oil," said Elizabeth Pancotti, a former Fed researcher and a senior executive at Groundwork Collaborative.

What the Fed can influence is demand. Warsh said the Fed raised rates to try to prevent the effects of tariff- and energy-induced inflation from spreading too deeply to other goods and services.

"What we can do and will do is ensure that any change in relative prices don't broaden out, don't have second- and third-order effects on the economy," he said.

What next?

Just how much does the Fed have to raise rates, or borrowing costs, to contain the spillover effects from supply shocks? That's where the consensus on Wall Street breaks down.

The Fed itself appears to be signaling that it will only require one more increase, and no more than two, to accomplish the job.

"We think one more will do the trick," said Sal Guatieri, senior economist at BMO Capital Markets. "We are not seeing lots of inflationary pressure outside of these supply shocks."

Take the labor market - traditionally a chief conveyor of high inflation. Labor costs are muted and have not been a big contributor to rising prices since the pandemic.

The cost of goods, meanwhile, has settled down after a big pop when the tariffs were first put in place. Prices of goods minus energy and food rose 0.7% in the 12 months that ended in August, down from a peak of 1.5% one year earlier.

For most of the last 15 years, goods prices usually declined each year, helping maintain low inflation.

"We see goods inflation going back to something negative," said Douglas of NISA.

The biggest source of inflation is services, and the rate of increase there has also slowed to close to prepandemic levels. Smaller increases in rents and home prices, the biggest expense for most people, are a big reason for that.

Aggressive strategy

Not everyone is convinced the Fed can wrestle inflation down to 2% with just one more rate hike. Some say it could take three or four increases.

Wall Street investors, for instance, are forecasting three more rate hikes between now and April, according to the closely followed FedWatch tool.

Alex Pelle, senior U.S. economist at Mizuho Securities, said the Fed has another problem: Inflation is not just rising because of supply-related issues tied to tariffs and oil.

The U.S. economy is also growing fast enough, he said, to drive up inflation through the normal demand channels: consumer spending and business investment, especially the boom in artificial intelligence.

"Demand is also excessive," said Pelle, who believes the economy is sturdy enough to absorb higher rates. "It's not going to go away completely on its own."

A more aggressive approach to raising interest rates would underscore the Fed's urgency to get to 2% inflation sooner rather than later.

Some analysts doubt Warsh is willing to wait two or three years to achieve that goal, based on his recent tough talk and his pre-Trump history of favoring an aggressive approach to fighting inflation.

"I have a hard time believing that Chairman Warsh will have that much patience for above-target inflation," said Stephen Stanley, chief U.S. economist at Santander Capital Markets.

Risk to the economy

That is exactly what worries a smaller but still sizable group of economists such as Daco of EY Parthenon. They contend the economy is not as strong as it looks.

A super-aggressive Fed bent on quelling inflation, Daco said, could deliver a stinging blow to the U.S. economy or even cause an outright recession. In such a scenario, the Fed would get to 2% inflation even more rapidly, but at the cost of millions of Americans losing their jobs or businesses.

"The Fed did not say the quiet part out loud," Daco said. "The reality is, the Fed is raising monetary policy to destroy demand to bring underlying inflation under control."

What would help the Fed avoid overshooting is a quick end to the Iran war and a drop in oil prices, but the conflict has already dragged on for more than six months.

"This is the big wild card for the Fed," Guatieri of BMO said. "The Fed can't ignore that."

-Jeffry Bartash
